title: Build a separate home for the opportunity the core business cannot value.
dek: In Chapter 10 of The Innovator's Dilemma, Clayton Christensen explains why disruptive opportunities need an organisation and decision process that can value what the established business must rationally reject.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: A disruptive opportunity can be real and still lose inside the organisation built to serve the current business. Give the new market a structure whose economics and values let it be judged fairly.

canon.heading: Give the disruptive opportunity an organisation that can believe in it.
canon.standfirst: Read the first bounded section of Chapter 10, "The Dilemmas of Disruptive Technology," from Clayton M. Christensen's The Innovator's Dilemma on PDF pages 256-275. Christensen turns the disruption problem into an organisation-design problem: the emerging offer needs processes, values, and ownership suited to its market.
canon.readerIntro: Read this as a study of structural fit. Mark where Christensen explains why the established organisation cannot evaluate a disruptive opportunity by its existing measures, how an independent unit can protect the new business from incumbent priorities, and what must remain connected to the core. Then diagnose one opportunity in your organisation: name the incumbent metric that would kill it, the separate structure it needs, and the evidence that should govern its next decision. Stop at PDF page 275.

blocks.label: 01 / The core business has a rational veto
paragraphs: The established business is not failing to understand the disruptive opportunity by accident. Its customers, margins, processes, and resource-allocation rules make the opportunity look unattractive.
Study the difference between an individual refusing to see a threat and a system whose definition of a good opportunity excludes the threat.

blocks.label: 02 / Give the new market its own logic
paragraphs: A disruptive initiative needs a structure that can value small markets, simpler products, uncertain demand, and different margins without being measured as a disappointing version of the core business.
Notice what must be separated so the new team can learn, and what must remain shared so it can still use the parent company's resources intelligently.

blocks.label: 03 / Design the decision process before the crisis
paragraphs: The organisation should decide in advance how a disruptive opportunity will be funded, staffed, measured, and protected from premature comparison with the incumbent business.
Choose one live opportunity and write the metric, owner, budget, and learning horizon that would let it be judged on the basis of the market it is trying to create.

closeReading: Why would the established organisation rationally reject the disruptive opportunity, even when its leaders can see the technology's potential?
Which existing customer, margin, or performance metric would make the new offer look weak or irrelevant?
What should a new disruptive unit share with the parent company, and what must it control for itself?
Choose one live opportunity. What structure, owner, budget, and time horizon would give it a fair test?
What evidence would show that the new organisation is learning toward a market rather than merely being protected from accountability?

principle.heading: Let the opportunity be judged by the market it is creating.
principle.body: A new-market idea often looks irrational when measured by the core business's customers, margins, and processes. Give it a structure with the resources and values needed to discover whether its different tradeoff can become valuable.
principle.example: A mature analytics company creates a small independent team for a low-cost, self-serve product. The team shares core data infrastructure but owns its roadmap, pricing tests, and success measure: repeat use among new customers rather than immediate enterprise revenue.
principle.practice: Choose one disruptive opportunity your organisation is considering. Write the core metric that would reject it, the customer it is meant to serve, the independent structure it needs, the shared resource it should borrow, and the first evidence that would justify another experiment.

output.heading: Build the conditions in which the new market can become legible.
output.body: When the core business cannot value an opportunity, change the organisation and the measure before concluding that the opportunity is weak.

signals.heading: Four current signals on how new markets are being made legible through separate products, channels, and decision systems.

fieldNotes.title: ChatGPT Ads expands discovery into 26 more markets
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI said ChatGPT Ads is expanding to 26 additional countries, bringing availability to 89 countries, after more than 100,000 advertisers used the platform. Ads appear on Free and Go plans while paid plans remain ad-free.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The move separates a new commercial system from the subscription core while using the same conversational surface. It is a live example of designing a distinct value proposition—discovery during consideration—rather than forcing advertising to imitate a conventional page or feed.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether clear separation from answers and privacy boundaries make the new market trustworthy enough to grow without weakening the product's core decision utility.

fieldNotes.title: OpenAI brings frontier models into Google Cloud's existing buying system
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI and Google Cloud announced that OpenAI models and Codex agentic workflows will come to Google Cloud's Model Garden, with access controls, data governance, and purchase through Google Cloud Marketplace planned for general availability in the coming weeks.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: Adoption is being routed through the environment enterprises already trust and budget for. The opportunity is not judged only as a better model; it gets a separate path to market while borrowing the incumbent's governance and procurement infrastructure.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether model choice inside an established cloud workflow produces durable usage, or whether governance and procurement friction still keep experimentation separate from production.

fieldNotes.title: Google gives small businesses an AI hub built around their existing tools
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Google announced a Gemini business landing page, brand-style controls, financial insight tools, templates, and connections to Google Business Profile, Google Ads, Workspace, Shopify, Canva, Dropbox, and other apps for small business owners.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: This is a product strategy signal: the new offer is made legible as a dedicated operating place for the small-business job, not as a general-purpose model asking owners to invent a workflow. Its value is easier to test when the tools, context, and audience are grouped around one market.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether the hub creates repeated business routines and measurable customer outcomes, rather than becoming another layer that owners must learn before they can get work done.

fieldNotes.title: OpenAI positions its life-sciences acquisition as a separate operating capability
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI announced the acquisition of Orchestra Bio, describing a combination of AI-powered operations and life-sciences R&D workflows to help biopharma teams accelerate drug development and advance new treatments.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: Entering a specialized value network requires more than pointing the general product at a new customer. A dedicated capability can learn the domain's evidence, processes, and buying logic while still drawing on the parent's platform and research resources.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether the new unit retains enough domain-specific autonomy to learn what biopharma customers value before being measured by the economics of the general AI business.

tweets.author: Shubh Agrawal
tweets.title: A startup wins when the new physics force a new story
tweets.summary: This is worth keeping because it treats narrative as part of the operating system, not decoration. A strange technical or market bet has to become desirable before incumbents copy it, and the company has to keep moving fast enough that the story remains attached to real progress.
tweets.text:
I joined Valley as a 21yo drop out, growth intern when we were at roughly $30k MRR and build systems that have closed over 800k mrr , booked thousands of meetings from inbound and outbound, here's what I tell startups -

full disclosure, I knew almost nothing substantial before joining https://t.co/Yswmr68WZY, it's just been figuring out what works after hundreds of mistakes and the help of an incredible team that allows you to essentially.. f*ck around and find out.

but if I were to help an early stage company build a repeatable, predictable motion - here's what I'd do:

1. Set up foundational GTM systems that compound with time on day one:

-> Founder led brand on any one platform, ur much better off being exceptional at one channel than trying to put 'good enough' content out there on multiple places.

"bUT sHUbH, i HAvE eXtRa tIMe tO MAke CoNTEnt oN mULTiPLe ChAnNeLs"

no you don't. If you do , produce better quality content in one channel, use rest of the time to engage with others. send people a text, comment under posts, quote reposts, interact with other people who comment. build a community, not audience.

this is your top of funnel.

-> Set up a hyper-valuable newsletter built for a very specific persona and send an email weekly. make it value driven, occasionally add stories.

Recruitment? send reports on job market, salary ranges, new profiles etc

Outreach? list building hacks, new updates, lessons and insights, outreach examples

design agency? send a culmination of great design examples.

2. Do NOT hire for marketing until BOFU to closed deal is solved:

Your initial few calls will come from word of mouth, referrals etc and if you've not been able to close deals consistently that way, don't have an offer people say yes to and stick around, do not hire someone in growth and marketing to fill your top of funnel.

Establish a motion where you're able to close deals and then and only then, get someone to help fill your calendar with more meetings.

3. $50k/mo is the stagnation zone for most b2b companies, especially agencies:

I've seen this pattern quite a bit, but most people that are able to grow to a certain scale hit roughly $40-60 k a month and stagnate. Most their customers come from word of mouth and referrals , this is the point where they need to spend thousands of dollars on risky marketing avenues like content, outreach, referrals etc to breakthrough - but they don't.

You're going to be stuck here for a long long time if you're not willing to lose some money to get ur next series of growth.

4. Focus early on AEO with bottom of funnel money keywords

Comparison pages, alternatives pages, listicles etc - skip TOFU keywords since AI answers have taken over them completely.

5. Build an outreach engine from day one on both LinkedIn and email - have atleast 5 domains and 15 inboxes warming up and sending at some capacity at all times, try to have 1-3 LinkedIN profiles sending outreach messages.

Start sending some form of outreach even if it is just saying hi. You don't have to try and sell everybody. Just connecting with people and being in front of them is the game here

Go win.
